questions.problem:
By finding the missing values in the ratio table below, determine which of the following graphs represents the given relationship.

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $5$ | $4$ |
|  | $8$ |
| $15$ |  |

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $5:4$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{5}{4}
$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\times 2}{4\times 2} & =\frac{10}{8} \\ \frac{5\times 3}{4\times 3} & =\frac{15}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $5$ | $4$ |
| $10$ | $8$ |
| $15$ | $12$ |

$$

$$

So, we have the following ordered pairs: $(5,4),$ $(10,8),$ $(15,12).$

Plotting these points on the coordinate plane, we get:

questions.worked_solution:
One of the points belonging to the graph is $(1\,000,200).$ Let's write the ratio $1\,000:200$ as a fraction:

$$
\frac{1\,000}{200}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $200:$

$$
\frac{1\,000÷200}{200÷200}=\frac{5}{1}
$$

 So the ratio of red paint to yellow paint is $5:1.$

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $2$ |
| $8$ |  |
|  | $6$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}4}:{\color{red}2}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}4}}{{\color{red}2}}
$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4\times 2}{2\times 2} & =\frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{4\times 3}{2\times 3} & =\frac{12}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our ratio table:

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $2$ |
| $8$ | $4$ |
| $12$ | $6$ |

So, we have the following ordered pairs: $(4,2),$ $(8,4),$ $(12,6).$

Plotting these points on the coordinate plane and connecting them with a straight line, we get the following graph:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152648/assets/8def1b37d62f91a16109db0da3287042fe5893b97bf447e6ee16946b3f8d4bfc.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Remember that we can place equivalent ratios in a ratio table, like the one below.

| $\color{blue}x$ | $\color{red}y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\color{blue}1$ | $\color{red}2$ |
| $\color{blue}2$ | $\color{red}4$ |
| $\color{blue}4$ | $\color{red}8$ |

By setting the values in the left column as $\color{blue}x$-coordinates and the values in the right column as the corresponding $\color{red}y$-coordinates, we can graph the points to represent a relationship between the ratios.

In this case, we have the following ordered pairs: $({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}2}),$ $({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}4}),$ $({\color{blue}4},{\color{red}8}).$

Plotting these points on a coordinate plane, we get the following graph:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152648/assets/0c4abb8d462730ed9b532feeca1e0a800f5376a978bfc799afb9d9a927ff310d.png)

Connecting the points gives us a straight line! Plotting equivalent ratios will *always* give a straight line. Furthermore, the straight line will *always* pass through the origin $(0,0).$
